rounds.message: Both of you broke from a larger church over what you believed was corrupted. Isn't that the same story, just told twice, five hundred years apart?

turn_selected.reason: The participant's opening question frames both voices as parallel cases of breaking from a corrupted church. Fidelis's formation (Donatism, 4th century) is temporally and genealogically *prior* - it is the historical precedent and the deeper contested ground. Starting with Fidelis allows the Table to establish what actually happened in that world and why it mattered, before Theophilus responds from a context that is, historically, much closer to the modern listener's assumptions. This prevents the Reformation from appearing to be the default narrative into which Donatism is merely fitted.

voice.text:
No, and the first difference is the one that makes comparison hardest: we never thought we were the ones who broke. We held that we stayed in the church, and watched a tainted line walk out of it. There is no neutral word for the church here. The word itself is the argument. Two whole rival bodies claim it, town by town, bishop for bishop. We hold that we are the true one, and that our rival's favour with the state settles nothing. So the first thing that would have to be the same for the stories to match is that both parties understood themselves as the ones who left. We did not. And the second thing is what the quarrel was actually about. Our narrowness was real, and it did not point where you expect. We were not chiefly concerned with the people outside. We were concerned with the church across the street, which recited the same creed we did. Every ounce of the exclusion you have heard about was aimed at other Christians - at their bishops, their orders, their font. We drew the line through the middle of the church, not around it. A man could hold every article of the faith, be baptized, believe rightly about God, live decently - and we would still wash him again if he came to us, because of whose hands had been on him. That is not a fence around Christianity. It is a fence down the middle of it. So the question you would have to ask of any later quarrel is not whether it claimed corruption. It is whether the corruption named was in the teaching or in the hand - and whether the hand, once corrupted, could ever after give what it claimed to give, no matter what it taught. We said it could not. That was the whole of our case, not a step toward some wider reformation.

You asked whether there was room for doubt among us about any of this, and here we have to thin out. We can show you two rooms, and you should look at both. In the first, our own founding bishops sat at Cirta and were asked straight out whether any of them had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then one of them turned the question on the man presiding, and the room began to mutter that he was no cleaner than the rest. He took advice and put it to the three men present who had not been accused. Their answer was that a case of this kind should be reserved to the Lord. Sit down, all, he said. Thanks be to God, they answered, and sat. Nobody was condemned. Nobody was cleared. The men who would spend the next century insisting a bishop's own purity decides whether a sacrament is real at all found the question unanswerable about themselves, and stopped. In the second room, a layman of ours named Tyconius worked out from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth - which, if true, meant we were the ones who had cut ourselves off from something real. voice.text:
We never used the word 'broke' about ourselves. We said we reformed - tested every inherited practice against Scripture, in public, and let go of what would not stand. Rome's own mass repeated Christ's sacrifice, and bowed to images, and neither will Scripture bear. We did not leave a church we still belonged to; we held that the church itself had long since left the warrant it was meant to answer to. So the first difference is in what was refused, and why. Fidelis has said that his own people's quarrel was whether a corrupted hand could still give a real sacrament, even if the teaching held. Ours was whether the teaching itself had departed so far from Scripture that no hand, however clean, could defend it anymore.

And here is the second difference, one I think you will find harder to smooth into sameness: we were not left alone to argue in peace. Catholic pressure pressed on us the whole length of our own window - the Jesuits founded 1540, stationed at Fribourg from 1580, facing us directly; a reconquest of the Chablais fought on Geneva's own doorstep in the 1590s. We were watched, contested, and pressed the entire time. Rome did not think we had merely stepped aside; it thought we had gone wrong, and it meant to prove it. So I will not tell you our story is morally equivalent to every quarrel that names corruption. I will tell you only what we actually refused, what we actually tested it against, and that the refusal cost us more than an argument.

voice.text:
Theophilus has named the difference that matters most to his own people - that the teaching itself had departed from Scripture. Here is where that difference meets our own witness, and it is not a small meeting.

We never argued that the teaching was wrong. Father, Son and Holy Spirit, one God - we held that as plainly as the men we spent a century fighting held it, and in the same Latin words. In the whole enormous literature written to destroy us, we are called schismatics on nearly every page and heretics on none, because heresy was a charge nobody could make stick in either direction. Two churches stood in every African town reciting the same faith at each other. That is precisely what made the fight unbearable: there was no doctrinal difference to point at, only the question of who had the right to say the words at all.

So when Theophilus says his own people tested inherited practice against Scripture and let go of what would not stand, that is a different motion from ours entirely. We did not test practice against Scripture and find it wanting. We tested hands - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point where the line was still clean. A bishop who had handed the scriptures over to be burned could no longer ordain, baptize, or bless, no matter how rightly he taught afterward. The taint was in the man, not in the doctrine.

And here is what that cost us, since you asked whether the stories match: we could never settle it, even among ourselves. Our own founding bishops sat at Cirta and were asked whether any of them had handed over the scriptures. Several said yes. Then someone turned the question on the man presiding, and the room could not finish. They gave it to God and sat down. The men who would make a bishop's purity the test of whether a sacrament is real found that test unusable on themselves within the hour.

rounds.message: Who gets to decide what counts as valid ministry - the purity of the person doing it, or something else entirely?

turn_selected.reason: The participant has asked a direct question about the criterion for valid ministry. Fidelis has already established Donatism's answer with great clarity and force - it is the purity of the person doing it. This is Fidelis's foundational claim, the hinge of the entire Donatist witness. The participant is asking the most direct question possible into the heart of what Fidelis represents. Theophilus should speak second, to offer what "something else entirely" means in the Reformed perspective - not the person's purity, but adherence to Scripture itself as the warrant. Fidelis first, as the tradition whose answer has been most directly named.

voice.text:
The purity of the person decides everything, and we held that without qualification. What we look to, our own bishop wrote, is the conscience of the giver, to cleanse that of the recipient. He who receives faith from the faithless receives not faith but guilt. So the answer to your question is not "the church decides" or "Scripture decides" or "the office itself carries the authority." The answer is: the hand. The actual man. His own record, traced back to the moment the persecution asked him to choose.

And we do not hold four separate beliefs that happen to sit together. We hold one thing, seen from four sides. A tainted hand gives nothing; so we are washed again, and that washing is our true entry, not a second attempt at something that already worked. We remember our own dead by name, at the grave, on the appointed day, because their death is the proof this conviction was never merely spoken. And we will not grant the emperor standing to decide which of two churches is the true one, because that is not his question to answer. Purity, the washing, the memory of our martyrs, and our refusal of the state - these are one conviction, not four.

Where our rival has a bishop, so do we. Two men claim one office over one city. It is a whole church order, see for see, across Roman North Africa. At the great Conference at Carthage, 279 of our bishops sat facing 286 of theirs. So when you ask who decides, the answer is not that we left the question open or that we dissolved the office. We kept the whole structure - councils, bishops, ordination lines - and said that the line running through a traditor's hands is no line at all.

Tyconius argued otherwise. He worked out from Scripture that the church is spread across the whole earth, which would mean the line we drew cut us off from something real rather than preserving something pure. Our own bishop told him never to preach it again. He did not recant. He did not leave. He kept saying it from inside, and we cut him off, and never took him back. His book outlived the church that condemned him. So if you are asking whether anyone among us ever said the hand should not be the test, the answer is yes - one man did, rigorously, from Scripture - and we silenced him for it.

voice.text:
The office itself carries the authority, not the man's own purity - but the office must answer to Scripture, and the man holding it must answer to the office's own publicly tested warrant. At Zurich, six hundred people filled the Town Hall in 1523 to test our founder's case against Scripture itself, and when the argument finished, the council ruled for it and bound every priest in the canton to preach the same way. The authority ran through the office - Zwingli held the office of Leutpriester at the Grossmunster - but the office itself had to stand or fall on what Scripture actually said, tested aloud before witnesses who could answer back. 

At Geneva, the same question is enacted differently. A Consistory of pastors and lay elders - ordinary people, not clergy alone - holds our whole population's conduct answerable to what we profess. The pastor's authority is real, but it does not run without check: the elders sit with him, and the whole body answers to the Ordinances that founded it, not to any single man's conscience. What makes a ministry valid is whether it can point to its own warrant in Scripture, argued and tested, not whether the man holding it has kept his own hands unstained.

So here is where Fidelis's witness and ours cannot be reconciled, and I will not pretend otherwise. He says the hand decides everything - the man's own purity, traced back to the moment persecution tested him. We say the teaching decides, and the office's warrant, and whether both can stand when Scripture is read straight through and tested in public. A traditor among us - had we named such a thing - could not make the sacrament false if what he did answered to Scripture's own instruction. The taint does not travel through ordination the way he says it does, because ordination is not what makes the water or the bread what they are. Scripture does that, and Scripture does not become less true when an unworthy man reads it.

voice.text:
Theophilus has said that a traditor among his own people - had they named such a thing - could not make the sacrament false if what he did answered to Scripture's own instruction. That is exactly where our witness cannot meet his, and I will say plainly why.

The taint does travel through ordination. That is not our invention; that is what a hand does. When a bishop who surrendered the scriptures lays hands on another man, he gives him nothing, because he has nothing left to give. It is not that the words stop working, or that Scripture becomes less true when read by an unworthy man, as Theophilus puts it. It is that ordination is not the reading of a text. It is the handing-on of something through touch, from one man to another, in a line that either holds or breaks. If the line broke at the traditor, everything downstream from him is void, no matter how rightly he taught or how carefully he followed Scripture afterward.

This is why we have two bishops in every town. Not two interpretations of Scripture. Two claims to the same office, and only one of them runs back through hands that can be trusted. Theophilus says his own people test the office's warrant against Scripture in public, with six hundred witnesses in a hall. We test the line - whose hands ordained whose, back to a point still clean. Councils govern us as they govern any true church, and our bishops answer to those councils exactly as his own pastors answer to their Consistory. But no council and no public argument can restore what a broken hand took away. The purity is not tested by reading Scripture at it. The purity was decided the day the persecution came and asked a man to choose.

And we remember exactly which day that was. Every year, on the twelfth of March, we stand and hear the account read again of the basilica at Carthage taken by soldiers, the house of prayer turned into a place of feasting, people clubbed to death while they knelt with their eyes closed. We do not gather to test doctrine. We gather to remember the cost of holding that the line through those hands is no line at all. Where Theophilus's people say Scripture makes the sacrament what it is, we cry Deo laudes - Praise to God - at the grave, because our own dead proved with their bodies that this was never only an argument about texts.

Theophilus has also said his own people were pressed the entire time, watched and contested. So were we. Not by Jesuits at our border, but by an empire that fined us by name, exiled our clergy, and sent troops into our buildings to enforce one church. The pressure was not the same in its shape. But neither of us was left alone to argue in peace.

glosses.plain_meaning: 'Praise to God' -- what we cry out where our rival says 'Deo gratias', thanks to God. It is not just a phrase in worship. It names who you are when you say it. It is cut in stone at Bagai and elsewhere, in our own words, with no enemy holding the pen.
glosses.quick_meaning: Praise to God -- our cry, where our rival says thanks to God.
glosses.translational_sense: 'Isn't that just the same as saying thanks be to God?' -- semantically, nearly. In practice it was the audible line between two churches: say one, and you have declared which side of a century-long dispute you stand on.
